schools.summary: Keil frames the reign as a double undertaking, to abolish idolatry and restore the worship of the LORD before throwing off Assyria; Ellicott parses the king's name, Yehizqiyahu, 'Strong is Iah,' noting the correspondence with 2 Kings 18:2.
Matthew Henry: Hezekiah applied himself at once to reform, for those who begin with God begin at the right end; the neglect of the temple under Ahaz was the very cause of the nation's calamities.
Clarke lays out the chapter's course in advance, from the opening of the doors to the rejoicing of king and people.
Gill, treating the two opening verses together, anchors the accession and refers to the parallel record.

themes: the meaning of the king's name

schools.summary: Ellicott notes the verse is identical with 2 Kings 18:3, the chronicler taking over the older verdict unchanged; Keil sets it at the head of the temple-purification, the root of which the whole reform is the fruit.
Clarke refers the reader to his note on the parallel at 2 Kings 18:3.

themes: did right in the sight of the LORD
the verse as title of the reform

schools.summary: Ellicott fixes 'the first month' as Nisan (not the first month of the reign), the doors as those Ahaz had closed (2 Chron 28:24), and 'repaired' as re-overlaying with metal (2 Kings 18:16); Keil weighs the same date and the verb used of Joash's restoration (2 Chron 24:12).
Gill adds that it was the first day of the first month, so that not a day was lost.

Keil places the assembly in the open eastern square before the temple, not the inner court, the king requiring the Levites to sanctify themselves before sanctifying the house; Ellicott confirms the eastern square (cf. Ezra 10:9).
Wesley: Hezekiah found Judah low and naked yet made it his first business to restore religion, not the civil interests of the kingdom.
Gill notes these were the persons who officiated in the temple service, now recalled to their work.

Ellicott traces 'filthiness' (niddah) through Leviticus and Ezekiel as personal impurity and anything loathsome, here the idols; Keil reads the charge with the fathers' whole sacrilege, noting that sacrifice had not wholly ceased but was offered on Ahaz's heathen altar.
Gill: the Levites were to sanctify themselves by washing their bodies and garments, that no defilement might cling to them.
Wesley names the 'filthiness' as the filthy altar Ahaz set in place of God's altar (2 Kings 16:11), with the idols.

Ellicott sharpens the Hebrew: 'trespassed' is 'dealt unfaithfully,' 'turned their backs' is literally 'gave neck' (cf. Jer. 2:27), a phrase whose ordinary sense is 'to put to flight'; the whole description falls upon Ahaz and his generation.
Gill takes 'our fathers' of the immediate ancestors, whose idolatry was the greatest evil and most provoking to God.
Wesley reads the turned back as wilful, obstinate contempt, a deliberate forsaking of God and his worship.

themes: the confession of the fathers' sin

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies each defaced ordinance: the porch as the sole entrance, the extinguished golden lamps, the cold incense-altar; the burnt-offerings on Ahaz's Syrian altar (2 Kings 16:15) counted as nothing because irregular.
Gill: to shut the doors of the porch was to bar all entrance to the temple.
Wesley notes Hezekiah says 'they,' not 'my father,' out of a son's tenderness for his father's name.

themes: a son's reticence over his father

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott trace the triad 'trouble, astonishment, and hissing' to the covenant curses of Deut. 28 and the threats of Jeremiah, reading 'as ye see with your eyes' as the visible ruin Ahaz brought by Aram, Israel, Edom, and the Philistines.
Clarke recalls the slaughter of 120,000 and captivity of 200,000 (2 Chron 28:6-8); Wesley draws the lesson that under God's rebukes we should ask whether we have neglected his ordinances.
Gill points to the invasions of Syrians, Israelites, Edomites, and Philistines as the appearing of that wrath.

themes: the wrath of God upon Judah

schools.summary: Keil binds the recital of the slain and captive to Hezekiah's resolve to make a covenant, marking the fatherly warmth of 'my sons' and the rare verb for negligence; Ellicott mends 'For' to 'And' and points back to the invasions of 2 Chron 28:5-8.
Gill refers the slaughter to the great numbers who fell before the kings of Syria and Israel.
Wesley notes the captives had in fact been presently released (2 Chron 28:14-15).

themes: the ground of a new beginning
the resolve to make a covenant

schools.summary: Ellicott fixes the phrasing: 'it is in mine heart' (cf. 1 Chron 22:7), the preposition 'for' in 'make a covenant with,' and 'turn away' as literally 'return,' the anger bidden to turn back (Num. 25:4).
Gill reads it as renewing a covenant after the manner of Asa and Jehoiada, to serve the LORD according to his will.
Clarke recovers the ancient terms of that national covenant, whose sign was circumcision and whose spirit was 'I will be your God; ye shall be my people.'

themes: the covenant purposed in the heart
turning away the wrath of God
the inward spring of the reform

schools.summary: Ellicott marks 'my sons' as a condescending endearment and the emphatic pronoun in 'you hath the LORD chosen,' judging the royal address a free composition after the manner of ancient historians; Keil names the fourfold office to which the Levites were chosen.
Gill hears the king speaking as a father, in the most tender and affectionate manner.
Wesley: he calls them sons though many were older, being a nursing father to them, and warns against slackness in sanctifying and in preparing the people.

themes: the dignity of the Levitical office
chosen to stand before the LORD
an appeal to honour, not fear

schools.summary: Ellicott confirms the pattern of two from each of the three subtribes, noting Mahath and Eden recur (2 Chron 31:13) and that these look like family names; Keil lays bare the deliberate symmetry, two from each ancestral house and each musical guild.
Gill goes through the whole roll of fourteen, house by house, from the Kohathites to Jeduthun.

themes: the willing response to the king

schools.summary: Keil continues the enumeration through the singers' houses and grounds the king's command 'by the words of the LORD' upon the Mosaic law (cf. 2 Chron 30:12); Ellicott fills in the pedigree of Elizaphan's house (Exod. 6:18, Num. 3:30).

themes: the singers' houses join the cleansing
the royal command grounded in God's word

schools.summary: Ellicott completes the fourteen with the houses of Heman and Jeduthun (Ethan), seven pairs in all (cf. 1 Chron 6:18-32); Keil sets down the same names in order.
Gill reckons Jeduthun the third of the principal singers and the same as Ethan, counting the two houses as the last of the seven pairs.

themes: singers among the first to labour

schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil both fasten on 'by the words of the LORD,' the royal mandate itself resting upon the written Law (cf. 2 Chron 30:12), so that the reform is obedience twice over, human authority moving under divine.
Gill notes they gathered their brethren and sanctified themselves, as they had been bidden.
Wesley pictures the homely labour of clearing dust, cobwebs, and rust, as well as idols and idolatrous altars.

themes: the command grounded in God's word

schools.summary: Keil describes priests bringing the uncleanness to the court and Levites carrying it to the Kidron, the Levites strictly kept from the holy place; Ellicott distinguishes the word for uncleanness and renders 'brook' as the Wady of Kidron (2 Kings 23:12).
Clarke lays out the sixteen days: eight for the courts, eight for the interior, the priests carrying the rubbish to the porch for the Levites.
Gill fixes the legal boundary, the priests into the holy place and, in necessity, even the most holy, to cleanse it.

themes: the filth carried to the Kidron
honouring the law even in cleansing

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott trace the two eight-day stages, the courts cleansed by the eighth of Nisan and the temple building by the sixteenth.
Gill notes they began on the first day of the first month, the month Nisan, called Ab by the Targum.
Wesley: 'a happy beginning of the new year!' — so should every year begin, with the purging of the year's defilements.

Keil names the rejected vessels — the copper altar, the brazen sea, the lavers (2 Kings 16:14-17); Ellicott notes the displaced altar of burnt-offering and the single 'table of the pile,' their metal tarnished by neglect.
Gill notes the Levites went in to Hezekiah in his palace to report the temple cleansed.

themes: a precise account of the work

schools.summary: Ellicott fixes 'cast away' (the word of 2 Chron 11:14), the vessels as the brazen altar, sea, and lavers, and 'prepared' as 'ordered aright'; Keil sets them sanctified and ready before the altar for the sacrifices of v.20.

Clarke gives the Targum's fuller paraphrase of vessels polluted, gathered, and replaced; Wesley draws the comfort that though the sanctuary's vessels be profaned a while, God will find a way to sanctify them again.
Gill, with Kimchi and the Targum, reads Ahaz's crime as removing the vessels to idolatrous uses, or profaning them, not casting away their gold.

Matthew Henry: atonement must be made for the sins of the last reign; it was not enough to lament and forsake, they brought a sin-offering — which obtains pardon only through Christ, made a sin-offering for us.
Ellicott explains the king gathered only the rulers of the city, having no time for a general summons, wishing to proceed at once with the sacrifices of expiation.
Gill: Hezekiah rose early, taking the first opportunity to worship and to set an example.

themes: the sin-offering as type of Christ

schools.summary: Keil notes the burnt-offerings are named first as in Leviticus though the sin-offering was presented before them; Ellicott calls it an extraordinary sacrifice for an extraordinary occasion (cf. Num. 23:1, Ezra 6:17), done in careful accordance with the Torah.
Clarke and Wesley agree the seven of each far exceeded the law's single victim because the sins were many and presumptuous, not sins of ignorance — atonement for kingdom, sanctuary, and people.
Gill reads the offerings as typical, respecting the sacrifice of the Messiah, seven of each because of the multitude of transgressions and long neglect.

Keil traces the blood from knife to altar for each kind of victim; Ellicott recovers the bowls of sprinkling, the throwing of blood against the altar (Lev. 8:19), and reads the symmetrical repetition as the writer's care to show the ritual exactly observed.
Gill notes the priests killed the seven bullocks first, in their appointed order.
Clarke reads the laying-on of hands as confession and vicarious substitution, the beasts dying in the owners' room; Wesley: the king and elders laid on hands in the name of the whole congregation.
Ellicott shows from Lev. 4:4 that the offerer pressed his hand on the victim's head, the king and congregation here doing it for the entire nation, and notes the classical word for the goats.
Gill: the goats were brought before king and congregation to make atonement for the sins of both.

themes: the guiltless dying for the guilty

schools.summary: Ellicott explains the blood on the horns and at the base of the altar (Lev. 4:30) and presses that 'for all Israel' includes the northern kingdom, pointing to the Passover invitation of 2 Chron 30:1; Keil fixes the king's command that widened the atonement.
Gill notes the priests killed the seven he-goats, the other victims having been slain before.

themes: the reach toward the northern tribes

schools.summary: Ellicott: Hezekiah restored the choral worship David established (1 Chron 23:5); this is the only place the Levitical minstrelsy is ascribed to the prophets Gad and Nathan, yet it was obeyed 'because it was divine,' the command of the LORD by his prophets.
Gill notes the cymbals, psalteries, and harps, the three principal instruments, disused under Ahaz.
Clarke grants David introduced the instruments by divine sanction, but protests their use in Christian worship as against the spirit of the gospel — 'away with such portentous baubles.'

debates.question: Was the temple's instrumental music of divine authority, and is it a pattern for worship?

sides.position: of divine authority, commanded through the prophets Nathan and Gad
David's own innovation, and no warrant for instruments in Christian worship

outliers.note: Turns the restored temple-music into a polemic against instruments in Christian worship, holding that where they most prevail there is least of the power of Christianity.

schools.summary: Keil describes the two companies — Levites with David's strings, priests with the trumpets — the trumpet-blast regulated by the stringed instruments; Ellicott marks the chronicler's evident interest in the temple's music.
Gill notes the Levites stood with the instruments David invented and ordered to be used.

themes: the law and the king sounding together

schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil both mark the exact coincidence — the song of Jehovah beginning at the instant the burnt-offering began, under the lead of the Davidic strings, the trumpets subordinate; the command repeated from v.21 to form the connection.
Gill: the burnt-offering was wholly devoted to the LORD, an acknowledgment of his sovereignty and goodness.
Wesley: even sorrow for sin must not put us out of tune for praising God; our praises attend his offering, accepted only in the virtue of it.

themes: accepted in the virtue of the offering
the psalms of David and Asaph

schools.summary: Keil renders the idiom 'the song was singing' for the body of singers, the worship continuing till the offering was finished; Ellicott reads instrument put for player and finds the verse a window on second-temple worship (cf. 2 Chron 7:5-6).
Gill: all the congregation worshipped, bowing their heads in adoration.

Keil marks the contracted verb for the ending of the sacrificial act, the king and all present kneeling; Ellicott renders 'bowed themselves' as 'bowed the knee' (Isa. 45:23), a sinking upon the knees, not a mere inclining of the head.
Gill notes they had made an end of offering both the sin-offering and the burnt-offering.

themes: the throne bowing with the people
answering the fathers who turned their backs

schools.summary: Keil reads the verse as a comprehensive conclusion, the Levites singing the words of David and Asaph and Asaph called a 'seer' (cf. 1 Chron 25:5); Ellicott allows that 'with the words of' may mean either chanting their psalms or singing according to their arrangements, and renders 'with gladness' as 'unto exultation.'
Gill takes the song, on Jarchi's guess, to be the psalm beginning 'O give thanks unto the LORD.'

debates.question: Does 'with the words of David and of Asaph' mean chanting their psalms or singing by their arrangement?

sides.position: chanting the actual psalms of David and Asaph
singing in accordance with the arrangements David and Asaph had made

themes: the psalms of David and Asaph
worship closing as it began, in song

schools.summary: Keil and Ellicott read 'ye have filled your hand to the LORD' as the language of consecration (Exod. 32:29, Lev. 7:37), applied to the whole assembly, and distinguish the thank-offerings from the wholly-consumed burnt-offerings, a token of greater self-denial.
Wesley reads the consecration as reconciliation accomplished, the burnt-offerings the most generous, being wholly offered to God.
Gill: the king 'answered,' that is, proceeded to speak.

debates.question: Is 'ye have filled your hand to the LORD' addressed to the priests or to the whole congregation?

sides.position: to the whole congregation, consecrated by their part in the solemnities
to the priests only, the king then turning to the people with 'come near'

schools.summary: Keil confirms the tally — seventy bullocks, a hundred rams, two hundred lambs — and calls it a very large number, brought spontaneously by the congregation.
Gill notes all were whole burnt-offerings, wholly devoted to the LORD, the offerers keeping no part to feast upon.

themes: the reform sunk into the nation's heart

schools.summary: Keil identifies the 'consecrated things' as the beasts for thank-offering (cf. 2 Chron 35:13), six hundred oxen and three thousand of the smaller cattle; Ellicott confirms them as the victims for the thank-offerings.
Gill notes the worshippers shared these peace-offerings, and that the number, smaller than in David's and Solomon's day, reflects a poorer nation and only two tribes.
Wesley takes the consecrated things as all the offerings devoted to God besides the burnt-offerings.

themes: God measures the heart, not the wealth

schools.summary: Keil explains the flaying fell to the priests in national sacrifices, the Levites assisting by necessity; Ellicott reads the pointed clause that the Levites 'were more upright in heart to sanctify themselves than the priests,' the priests being more deeply involved in the corruption of the last reign.
Wesley reads 'too few' of the priests fit and sanctified, necessity excusing the Levites' help; Clarke dwells on the priests' backwardness and the Levites' readiness.
Gill notes the flaying of the burnt-offerings was properly the priests' work, and they were too few.

outliers.note: Turns the priests' backwardness into a warning that a rich, worldly priesthood is unfavourable to religion, the higher orders often less concerned for it than the lower.

themes: the Levites more upright than the priests

schools.summary: Ellicott identifies the accompaniments — the fat of the peace-offerings burned on the burnt-offerings (Lev. 3:5) and the drink-offerings (Num. 15:1) — as a further reason the Levites helped; Keil sets the abundance within the summary that 'the service of the house of the LORD was set in order.'
Gill notes the meat-offerings, drink-offerings, and fat of the peace-offerings made a great deal of business needing many hands.

themes: worship restored to its whole round

schools.summary: Keil grounds the joy in what 'God had prepared for the people' by the cleansing and restored worship, heightened by its suddenness; Ellicott renders 'on a sudden happened the matter' and finds the hand of God in the speed of the revolution.

Clarke: God prepared their hearts to bring so great a reformation in so short a time, the king's influence the grand spring under God; Wesley reads the sudden change from Ahaz's idolatry as plainly the work of the Holy Spirit changing hearts.
Gill notes Hezekiah and all the people rejoiced to see things go on so well.

debates.question: Does 'God had prepared' mean he prepared the ordinances for the people, or prepared the people themselves?

sides.position: God prepared / set in order the long-suspended ordinances for the people
God prepared the people themselves, turning their hearts

themes: the suddenness as the hand of God
